findings: The scorer underestimates contradiction risk when a cut leaves a short clause fragment (a subject/NP or function-word-only span) that lacks its predicate, auxiliary, negation scope, or required complement; such pre-cut fragments, read alone, often assert something the rest of the sentence later reverses.

The scorer undervalues cohesion loss from splitting heads from their required complements (prepositions and their objects, 'of' phrases, verb complements, or a main noun and its postnominal modifiers); cuts that sever these relationships often degrade joined translation quality.

diagnosis.why: The inserted principle forbidding cuts that separate heads from required complements caused the model to avoid splitting prepositional/complement spans and instead shift cuts earlier (often between verbs/subjects and following prepositions), which helps cohesion for long pieces but produced many harmful single-word or very-short pieces — hurting the ≤3 and ≤7 bins and yielding slightly more worse (199) than better (167) pairs.
diagnosis.lesson: A later revision should respect that banning head–complement splits can force cuts into short-span head–dependent links (creating isolated words or subject–verb splits); avoid changes that improve long-span cohesion while degrading small-bin coherence.
